analogy.p: Imagine a cinema ticket office that only records which ROW each person sat in, not the exact seat. To guess the average position of the audience you pretend everyone in a row sat in the middle seat of that row, then average those middle seats weighted by how many people were in each row. The class is the row, the midpoint is the middle seat and the frequency is the number of people in the row. It breaks down because in a cinema seats are fixed and countable, whereas a continuous measurement such as height could take any value inside the class and the real mean could be above or below the guess.

bullets: **Grouped frequency table**: a table with classes (like 160 < h ≤ 170) and the number of data values in each class (the frequency).
Grouping is used for **continuous data** and for **discrete data with a wide spread** (for example marks out of 100 grouped in tens).
The original raw values cannot be recovered from the table, so the mean, median and range from it are **estimates**.
Edexcel Higher expects you to **estimate the mean** from a grouped table, **identify the modal class** and the **class containing the median**, and use the table to answer comparison questions.
Always read the table headings and units first, and check that the frequencies add up to the total number of items in the data set (for example 40 students).
Grouped tables are the starting point for later topics: **cumulative frequency graphs**, **box plots** and **histograms** all use the same grouped data.
core.h: What grouped data is and why we use it
core.p: When a data set is large, or the values are **continuous** (such as height, mass, time or length), it is not sensible to list every single value. Instead the data is sorted into **class intervals** and the **frequency** of each class is recorded in a **grouped frequency table**. The price of this tidy summary is that the individual values are lost: we only know how many values fell in each class, not what they were. Because of this, any average we calculate from a grouped table can only be an **estimate**, and the specification expects you to say so.

bullets: **Lower class boundary** = the smallest value the class starts from (150 in 150 < h ≤ 160). **Upper class boundary** = the largest value in the class (160).
**Class width** = upper boundary − lower boundary. For 150 < h ≤ 160 the width is 160 − 150 = 10.
Classes for continuous data must join up with no gaps: the upper boundary of one class is the lower boundary of the next.
Classes of **equal width** are easier to work with; if widths are unequal you need **frequency density** (see the histograms topic).
If the data is written as discrete groups such as 1-5, 6-10, 11-15, the true boundaries for continuous measurement would be 0.5, 5.5, 10.5, 15.5, so read the question carefully.
A value exactly on a boundary goes into the class whose inequality includes it (the ≤ side), for example 160 cm goes in 150 < h ≤ 160.
core.h: Class intervals, class boundaries and class width
core.p: Each row of a grouped table is a **class interval** written with inequality symbols such as 150 < h ≤ 160. This means h is greater than 150 and less than or equal to 160, so 150 itself belongs in the class below and 160 belongs in this class. Writing classes with inequalities means there are no gaps and no overlaps, so every value belongs to exactly one class. The **class width** tells you how wide the class is and is found by subtracting the lower boundary from the upper boundary.

bullets: **Midpoint = (lower boundary + upper boundary) ÷ 2**.
Example: for 140 < h ≤ 150 the midpoint is (140 + 150) ÷ 2 = 290 ÷ 2 = 145.
Example with unequal width: for 30 < t ≤ 60 the midpoint is (30 + 60) ÷ 2 = 45, not 35.
Check your midpoints by making sure they go up in even steps when the class widths are equal (145, 155, 165, 175, 185).
The midpoint always lies **inside** the class and never on a boundary.
Using the midpoint assumes the values are spread **evenly** across the class, so some are above and some below the midpoint and the errors roughly cancel.
core.p: To calculate with a grouped table we need a single value to stand for every item in a class. We use the **midpoint** of the class, because it is the best single guess when the values could be anywhere in the class. The midpoint is exactly halfway between the lower and upper boundaries. It is the key idea that makes an estimate of the mean possible.

bullets: Step 1: add a column for the **midpoint x** and work out each midpoint.
Step 2: add a column for **f × x** and multiply the frequency by the midpoint on every row.
Step 3: find the **total of the frequency column** (Σf) and the **total of the f × x column** (Σfx).
Step 4: **estimated mean = Σfx ÷ Σf**. Include units.
Worked data (heights): fx values 580, 1550, 2310, 1400, 740 sum to 6580; Σf = 40; mean ≈ 6580 ÷ 40 = **164.5 cm**.
Sense check: the mean must lie between the lowest midpoint (145) and the highest midpoint (185), and usually near the class with the highest frequency.
Method marks: M1 for the midpoints, M1 for fx products, M1 for dividing a total by a total, A1 for the answer. Showing the table secures most of these marks.
Do **not** divide by the number of classes (5) and do **not** add up the midpoints: you must weight by frequency.
core.h: Estimating the mean step by step
core.p: The mean of ungrouped data is the sum of the values divided by how many there are. For grouped data we do not know the values, so we replace each value by its class midpoint. Each class then contributes (frequency × midpoint) to the total, and we divide by the total frequency. This is why the method is written **estimated mean = Σ(f × x) ÷ Σf**, where f is the frequency and x the midpoint. Setting the working out in a table keeps it organised and earns method marks even if you slip on the arithmetic.

bullets: Reason to quote: **"the actual values are not known, we have used the midpoint of each class instead"**.
The true mean could be **higher or lower** than the estimate, and from the table alone we cannot tell which.
The narrower the classes, the closer the estimate is to the true mean, because the midpoint is a better stand-in for each value.
If an exam asks "Is your answer an overestimate or an underestimate?" there must be extra information (for example all values in a class are below the midpoint); otherwise say you cannot be sure.
An estimate of a **range** is the greatest possible range: upper boundary of the top class − lower boundary of the bottom class (190 − 140 = 50 cm).
The least possible range is found from the lowest value of the top class to the highest value of the bottom class (180 − 150 = 30 cm in the height example, strictly just over 30).
core.h: Why the answer is only an estimate
core.p: A grouped table tells us only how many values are in each class. Within a class, the real values could be anywhere, and we have assumed they all equal the midpoint. In real data some values are higher and some lower than the midpoint, so the answer will be close to the real mean but not exactly equal to it. Mark schemes reward the word **estimate** and a reason in terms of the data being grouped.

bullets: **Modal class = the class interval with the largest frequency**.
In the height example, the highest frequency is 14, so the modal class is **160 < h ≤ 170**.
Give the **class**, not the frequency. A common error is writing 14.
If two classes tie for the highest frequency, the data is **bimodal** and both classes are modal classes.
When class widths are **unequal**, the modal class is the class with the highest **frequency density** (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.
The modal class can be written as an inequality or as the range of values, for example 160 to 170 cm.
core.p: The mode is the most common value, but in a grouped table we cannot see single values. Instead we state the **modal class**, which is the class with the **highest frequency**. This is the simplest average to read from a table because no calculation is needed. It is also the only average that can be found for categorical data, though in grouped tables it is always a class.

bullets: Position of the median for n values = **(n + 1) ÷ 2** (many mark schemes also accept n ÷ 2 for large data sets).
Height example: n = 40, so the median is at (40 + 1) ÷ 2 = **20.5th value**.
The 20.5th value is bigger than 14 and not bigger than 28, so it lies in the third class: **160 < h ≤ 170**.
The median class is often the same as the modal class, but not always, so work it out separately.
Writing the running totals next to the table is the best way to show your working for a mark.
An **estimate of the median value** requires a cumulative frequency graph (a different topic) and is not read from the table directly.
core.p: The median is the middle value when the data is in order. Because we cannot see the individual values, we can only find the **class that contains the median**. First find the position of the median, then use the running total (cumulative frequency) of the frequencies to see which class that position falls in. This is the same idea that a cumulative frequency graph uses to find an estimate of the median.

bullets: **Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width**.
Example: 5 values in the class 30 < t ≤ 60 gives frequency density 5 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.17, while 15 values in 10 < t ≤ 20 gives 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5.
With unequal widths the **modal class** is the class with the highest frequency density.
The estimated mean uses midpoints exactly as before. Class width does not change the method for the mean.
The **median class** still uses the running total of frequencies, because position in the ordered list does not depend on class width.
In the time example: classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-60 have midpoints 5, 15, 25 and 45.
core.h: Unequal class widths and the modal class
core.p: Sometimes the classes in a grouped table have different widths, for example 0 < t ≤ 10, 10 < t ≤ 20, 20 < t ≤ 30, 30 < t ≤ 60. A wider class will usually collect more values simply because it covers more numbers, so the highest frequency does not mean the busiest class. To compare fairly we use **frequency density**. This links grouped data to histograms, where the height of each bar is frequency density.

bullets: Find which class contains the given value and what fraction of that class lies beyond it.
Example: how many students are taller than 175 cm? The class 170 < h ≤ 180 has 8 students and 175 is exactly halfway, so about half (4) are taller than 175.
Add the full classes above: 4 students in 180 < h ≤ 190. Total ≈ 4 + 4 = **8**.
Write the assumption: **"assuming the heights in the class are evenly spread"**.
Unequal fractions: for 168 in the class 160 < h ≤ 170 the fraction above is (170 − 168) ÷ 10 = 0.2, so 0.2 × 14 = 2.8 students, about 3.
Your answer should be a sensible whole number of people where counts are involved, though showing a decimal first is fine.
This links directly to cumulative frequency graphs, which do the same estimate by reading a graph.
core.h: Estimating how many values are above or below a given value
core.p: A Higher tier question may ask you to estimate the number of data items above, below or between certain values. To do this you assume the values in the class are **spread evenly**, so the proportion of the class above a point is the same as the proportion of the class width above it. Whole classes beyond the point are counted in full. The word **estimate** and the assumption of even spread are what examiners look for in the answer.

bullets: Compare **averages**: "On average the boys are taller because the estimated mean of 168.2 cm is greater than the girls' 164.5 cm."
Compare **spread**: the group with the larger (greatest possible) range is more spread out; a smaller range means more **consistent** data.
Always mention the **context** (heights, times, scores) and use numbers from the data.
Say "estimated" when quoting a mean or range from grouped data.
Do not compare frequencies when the group sizes differ; compare means or proportions instead.
A comparison needs both groups mentioned in one sentence using words such as "whereas", "higher than" or "less than".
core.p: Questions often give two grouped tables and ask you to compare the distributions. You should compare an **average** and a **measure of spread**, and always write the comparison in the context of the question. The estimated mean from each table gives the average. For spread you can use the estimated range, or the modal class and how widely the classes are populated. Use comparison words such as "higher", "more consistent", "wider spread".

bullets: **Frequency polygons**: plot (midpoint, frequency) points and join them with straight lines.
**Cumulative frequency**: plot cumulative frequency against the **upper boundary** of each class (not the midpoint) to estimate median and quartiles.
**Histograms**: with unequal widths the vertical axis is frequency density; area is proportional to frequency.
**Statistics calculators**: the stats mode lets you enter midpoints and frequencies, then returns x̄ directly. Always write the method down too.
Ungrouped frequency tables use the same Σfx ÷ Σf method but with the exact values in place of midpoints, giving an **exact** mean.
Expect grouped data questions to be worth **2 to 5 marks** and to appear on all three papers (Paper 1 non-calculator can use easy numbers).
core.h: Links to other topics and using a calculator
core.p: Grouped data connects several parts of the Edexcel specification. Midpoints appear again when drawing frequency polygons, where you plot frequency against class midpoint. Running totals become the cumulative frequency graph. Frequency density leads to histograms. A scientific calculator can speed up the arithmetic, but you must still show the table or the individual products for method marks.

bullets: Check Σf equals the stated number of items (40 in the example).
Check each midpoint is halfway: add the boundaries and halve.
Check each product f × x using estimation, for example 14 × 165 ≈ 14 × 160 = 2240, so 2310 is sensible.
If the mean is outside the range of midpoints, an error has been made.
Give the answer with units (cm, minutes, marks) and to a sensible accuracy, usually 1 decimal place or as the question requires.
Non-calculator papers use friendly numbers, so look for easy multiples when multiplying.
core.p: A good student checks every grouped-data answer in three ways: that the frequency total matches the question, that the mean lies between the smallest and largest midpoint, and that the answer has units and the word estimate where needed. These quick checks catch the majority of lost marks. Practising with real tables until the layout becomes automatic is the best preparation.

exam: **Command words**: 'Work out an estimate for the mean' means use midpoints and Σfx ÷ Σf; 'Write down the modal class' means one class only; 'Find the class that contains the median' means use running totals.
A typical estimate-of-the-mean question is **3 or 4 marks**: 1 mark for midpoints, 1 for the f × x products, 1 for the total of fx divided by total f, 1 for the answer.
Always **draw the table** with extra columns for x and f × x. Even if the final answer is wrong you earn method marks for correct working.
Write **'estimate'** in your answer and give units: 'estimated mean = 164.5 cm'.
A **1 or 2 mark** reason question: 'Why is your answer only an estimate?' Model phrase: **'Because the data is grouped, so we do not know the actual values; we used the midpoints.'**
For 'Is the actual mean greater or less than your estimate?' only commit to an answer if the question provides information; otherwise say it could be either.
For 'Find the median class' write the position first (for example 20.5th), then show the running totals 4, 14, 28 and state the class.
For 'estimate the number of items greater than a value', state the assumption **'evenly spread within the class'** and show the fraction of the class used.
Comparison questions (2 marks): compare an average AND a spread, with figures, in context, using the word 'estimated'.
On Paper 1 (non-calculator) numbers are chosen to multiply easily; on Papers 2 and 3 you may use the calculator's stats mode but still show the table.
Check that your estimated mean lies between the smallest and largest midpoint; if not, you have made an error.

mistakes.r: Divide by the total frequency Σf (the number of data items, 40 in the example).
mistakes.w: Dividing the sum of fx by the number of classes (for example ÷ 5).

mistakes.r: Use the midpoint (lower + upper) ÷ 2 for x.
mistakes.w: Using the class boundaries or the class width instead of the midpoint in the f × x column.

mistakes.r: State the class itself, for example 160 < h ≤ 170.
mistakes.w: Giving the frequency (14) as the modal class.

mistakes.r: Write estimate and explain that the data is grouped so the exact values are unknown.
mistakes.w: Stating the mean exactly with no mention of an estimate.

mistakes.r: Use the running total (cumulative frequency) to find which class contains the 20.5th (or 20th) value.
mistakes.w: Finding the median position as 40 ÷ 2 = 20 and then picking the 20th value from the frequency column.

mistakes.r: Use the highest frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
mistakes.w: Choosing the class with the highest frequency as the modal class when the class widths are unequal.

mistakes.r: Weight each midpoint by its frequency: Σfx ÷ Σf.
mistakes.w: Adding the midpoints and dividing by the number of classes.
Calculating the midpoint of 30 < t ≤ 60 as 35 or 30.

summary: You must be able to read a grouped frequency table, find midpoints, estimate the mean using Σfx ÷ Σf, and identify the modal class and the class containing the median, explaining that results are estimates. It matters because grouped data underpins cumulative frequency, histograms and many comparison questions on all three papers.

terms.d: A table that shows how many data values fall in each class interval.
A range of values written with inequality symbols, such as 150 < h ≤ 160, into which data is grouped.
The number of data values that fall in a class or take a particular value.
Upper class boundary minus lower class boundary.
The lowest or highest value that belongs to a class interval.
The value halfway between the lower and upper boundaries of a class: (lower + upper) ÷ 2.
An approximation of the mean from grouped data found using Σ(f × x) ÷ Σf, where x is the class midpoint.
The symbol meaning 'the sum of'; Σf is the total frequency and Σfx the total of the f × x column.
The class interval with the highest frequency (or highest frequency density if the classes have unequal widths).
The class interval that contains the median, found using the position (n + 1) ÷ 2 and the running total of frequencies.
Data that can take any value in a range, such as height, mass or time, which is measured rather than counted.
Data that can take only particular values, usually counted, such as the number of goals.
Frequency divided by class width; used for the heights of histogram bars.
An approximate value found using assumptions, here that all the values in a class equal the midpoint or are evenly spread.
The running total of the frequencies up to the end of a class.

worked.q: The table shows the heights of 40 students. 140<h≤150: 4; 150<h≤160: 10; 160<h≤170: 14; 170<h≤180: 8; 180<h≤190: 4. Work out an estimate for the mean height. [4 marks]
The times, t minutes, taken by 35 people to complete a task: 0<t≤10: 6; 10<t≤20: 15; 20<t≤30: 9; 30<t≤60: 5. (a) Find the class containing the median. (b) Work out an estimate for the mean. [5 marks]
steps: 18 is more than 6 but not more than 21, so the median is in 10<t≤20.

worked.ans: (a) About 8 students (assuming heights are evenly spread in each class). (b) We do not know the actual values, only the class each belongs to, so the mean is an estimate using midpoints.
worked.q: Using the heights table above, (a) estimate how many students are taller than 175 cm, and (b) explain why your answer for the mean is only an estimate. [4 marks]
steps: (a) 175 is the midpoint of 170<h≤180, which has 8 students.
Assuming the heights are evenly spread in the class, half of them, 4, are taller than 175.
All 4 students in 180<h≤190 are taller than 175, so total = 4 + 4 = 8.
(b) The data is grouped, so the actual heights are not known; each height has been replaced by the class midpoint.
